lead: Density is the mass a fluid packs into one cubic metre. Everything else in this chapter is built from it: multiply by g and you get specific weight, divide by water's density and you get specific gravity, and squeeze the fluid to get bulk modulus and compressibility. Engineers use these numbers daily — an oil supplier quotes specific gravity, a dam designer needs specific weight, a hydraulic press designer needs to know how much the oil shrinks under pressure. Get density right and the rest is arithmetic.
prereq: You need: Ch 1.1 for the continuum idea and the meaning of a fluid.

blocks.text: Mass density is the mass of fluid in unit volume. It answers one question: how much matter sits inside one cubic metre?

blocks.where: ρ (Greek rho) is mass density in kg/m³; m is the mass in kg; V is the volume in m³.

blocks.text: Specific volume is the same idea turned upside down: the volume that one kilogram occupies. Steam tables and refrigeration work use it more than density.

blocks.where: v is specific volume in m³/kg; ρ is density in kg/m³.

blocks.text: Water at 4 °C has ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Mercury has ρ = 13600 kg/m³. Air at 20 °C and normal atmospheric pressure has ρ ≈ 1.2 kg/m³. Air is roughly 800 times lighter than water, which is why a balloon of air feels empty but a balloon of water does not.

Density of a gas falls when it expands and rises when it is compressed. Density of a liquid changes very little, so most liquid problems treat ρ as a constant. Water at the bottom of a 100 m dam has a density only about 0.05 % higher than at the surface (a rise of roughly 0.5 kg/m³ on 1000 kg/m³). Even at 1 km depth the rise is only about 0.5 %.
Specific weight is the weight of fluid in unit volume. Weight is a force, so specific weight is a force per volume, not a mass per volume.

blocks.where: γ (Greek gamma) is specific weight in N/m³; ρ is density in kg/m³; g is gravitational acceleration, 9.81 m/s².

blocks.text: Do not swap the two. Density is in kg/m³ and is a property of the fluid alone. Specific weight is in N/m³ and depends on where you are: the same water on the Moon has the same density but about one-sixth the specific weight, because g changes.
Specific gravity is a pure ratio. It compares the fluid with water at 4 °C, so it has no unit at all.

blocks.where: SG is specific gravity (dimensionless); ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³; γ_water = 9810 N/m³.

blocks.text: Specific gravity is what the petrol pump, the coolant bottle and the battery shop actually talk about. Petrol has SG about 0.72, so one litre has a mass of about 0.72 kg and weighs about 0.72 × 9.81 ≈ 7.1 N. Mercury has SG 13.6, which is why a 760 mm mercury column balances the whole atmosphere. Battery acid is checked by SG because a charged battery's acid is denser than a discharged one.
Bulk modulus measures how strongly a fluid resists being squeezed. Apply a pressure rise, watch the volume shrink, and the ratio tells you the stiffness.
K = − V dp / dV = ρ dp / dρ
blocks.where: K is the bulk modulus in Pa (or N/m²); dp is the pressure rise; dV is the change in volume; V is the original volume. The minus sign keeps K positive because volume falls as pressure rises.

blocks.text: For finite changes the same relation is written K ≈ − Δp / (ΔV/V). The fraction ΔV/V is the volumetric strain, so K is pressure divided by strain — exactly like Young's modulus for a solid, but for volume instead of length.
Compressibility is simply the reciprocal. It tells you how much volume shrinks per unit pressure.

blocks.where: β (Greek beta) is compressibility in Pa⁻¹ (or m²/N); K is bulk modulus in Pa.

blocks.text: Water has K ≈ 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa, so β ≈ 4.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹. A pressure rise of one atmosphere (about 10⁵ Pa) shrinks water by only about 0.005 %. That is why liquids are called incompressible in normal work. Mercury is stiffer still; air has K ≈ 10⁵ Pa, about four orders of magnitude (roughly 20 000 times) softer than water.

A gas has no single K. Squeeze it slowly and heat escapes, so the process is isothermal and K = p for an ideal gas. Squeeze it fast and heat stays in, so the process is adiabatic and K = γp, where γ is the ratio of specific heats (1.4 for air). Always state the process. See Unit 3 for compressible flow, where these ideas become essential.

figure.caption: Density sits at the root; multiplying by g gives specific weight, dividing by water's density gives specific gravity, and a pressure test gives bulk modulus and its reciprocal. Notice that specific weight is the only branch that depends on g and is written with newtons (N/m³); bulk modulus is written in pascals (N/m²), a pressure.

spec.aria: A tree rooted at density, with branches to specific weight (multiply by g), specific gravity (divide by water density), bulk modulus (from a pressure test) and compressibility (reciprocal of bulk modulus), each with its formula and units.

examples.question: An oil used in a hydraulic press has density 880 kg/m³. Take g = 9.81 m/s² and ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³. (a) Find its specific weight and specific gravity. (b) When the press is loaded, a pressure rise of 2 MPa reduces the oil volume by 0.1 %. Find the bulk modulus and the compressibility of the oil.
steps: List the data: ρ = 880 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s², ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³, Δp = 2 MPa = 2 × 10⁶ Pa, ΔV/V = 0.1 % = 0.1/100 = 0.001.
(a) Specific weight: γ = ρ g = 880 × 9.81 = 8632.8 N/m³. Round to 8.63 kN/m³.
(a) Specific gravity: SG = ρ / ρ_water = 880 / 1000 = 0.88. It is dimensionless, so write no unit.
(b) Bulk modulus from the finite-change form: K = Δp / (ΔV/V) = 2 × 10⁶ / 0.001 = 2 × 10⁹ Pa, that is 2 GPa.
Check the size: 2 GPa is close to water's 2.2 GPa, so this oil behaves like a stiff liquid, and a 2 MPa load shrinks it by only a thousandth of its volume.
examples.answer: γ = 8.63 kN/m³, SG = 0.88, K = 2 × 10⁹ Pa (2 GPa) and β = 5 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹.

code.code:
rho = 880.0
g = 9.81
rho_w = 1000.0
dp = 2.0e6
strain = 0.1 / 100.0
gamma = rho * g
sg = rho / rho_w
K = dp / strain
beta = 1.0 / K
print("gamma =", round(gamma, 1), "N/m3")
print("SG =", round(sg, 2))
print("K =", K, "Pa")
print("beta =", beta, "1/Pa")

traps: Writing specific gravity with a unit. SG is a ratio of two densities, so it is plain 0.88, not 0.88 kg/m³.
Putting ρ_water = 1 in place of 1000 kg/m³. In SI, water is 1000 kg/m³ and 9810 N/m³; the value 1 belongs only to the cgs system or to SG itself.
Confusing density (kg/m³) with specific weight (N/m³). A question that asks for specific weight wants the g multiplied in.
Dropping the minus sign in K = −V dp/dV. Volume decreases when pressure increases, so without the minus sign you would report a negative stiffness.
Using K = p for a gas in every case. That holds only for an isothermal process; adiabatic compression gives K = γp, and the answer differs by 40 % for air.

quiz.q: Define mass density and state its SI unit.
quiz.a: Mass density is mass per unit volume, ρ = m/V. Its SI unit is kg/m³.

quiz.q: Why is specific gravity dimensionless while specific weight is not?
quiz.a: Specific gravity is the ratio of two densities (fluid to water), so the kg/m³ cancel and no unit remains. Specific weight is a weight per volume, ρg, and weight is a force, so it carries N/m³.

quiz.q: A liquid has specific gravity 1.26. Find its density and its specific volume. Take ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³.
quiz.a: ρ = SG × ρ_water = 1.26 × 1000 = 1260 kg/m³. Specific volume v = 1/ρ = 1/1260 = 7.94 × 10⁻⁴ m³/kg.

quiz.q: Water (K = 2.2 × 10⁹ Pa) fills a rigid steel cylinder completely. The pressure is raised by 5 MPa. Find the fractional volume decrease.
quiz.a: ΔV/V = Δp/K = 5 × 10⁶ / 2.2 × 10⁹ = 2.27 × 10⁻³, that is about 0.23 %. Compressibility β = 1/K = 4.55 × 10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹.

quiz.q: Two students compute the bulk modulus of air at 1 atm. One uses K = p and the other K = 1.4p. Both can be right. Explain.
quiz.a: For an ideal gas, bulk modulus depends on the process. Slow compression lets heat escape: isothermal, K = p ≈ 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa. Fast compression traps heat: adiabatic, K = γp = 1.4 × 1.01 × 10⁵ ≈ 1.42 × 10⁵ Pa. A gas has no single K until the process is stated; a liquid's K is a property of the fluid almost independent of process.

quiz.q: A tank of oil is weighed on the Moon (g = 1.62 m/s²) and on Earth. Which quantities change: mass, density, specific weight, specific gravity?
quiz.a: Mass and density do not change, since they do not involve g. Specific gravity does not change either, because it is a density ratio. Specific weight does change: γ = ρg becomes 1.62/9.81 ≈ 0.165 of its Earth value.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern hydraulic systems run at 30 MPa and above, where oil compressibility stops being negligible and gives the fluid a spring-like stiffness that sets the natural frequency of the press or the actuator. Search for "bulk modulus hydraulic fluid" and "effective bulk modulus" — the pipe walls and trapped air lower it well below the oil's own value, and that is why air bleeding matters. Water hammer in Unit 4 is the same physics arriving as a pressure surge.
